title: How can objects express culture and identity?
essentialQuestion: How do ordinary things carry meaning for people and communities?
learningGoal: Explain how one object can have different meanings for different people and in different contexts.

warmUp.question: Why might a person keep an old object for a long time?

evidence.label: Fictional example created for this lesson.
evidence.question: What does each note tell you about the bag?

cards.title: Woven bag
items: Made by a community craft group
A pattern of triangles and lines on one side

cases.name: Owner's note
cases.body: “My aunt gave me this when I started at a new school.”

sections.heading: One object can have many meanings
sections.text: Look at the woven bag in the evidence. The seller says it is made for carrying food and books. That is its practical use. The owner says an aunt gave it to them when they started at a new school, so the bag also holds a memory. The makers, a craft group, learned the pattern from older weavers. For them, the bag shows a skill. It is one bag, but each person sees it from a different perspective. To understand an object, you need its context: who made it, who uses it, and why.
sections.simpler: Look at the woven bag. The seller says it carries food and books. That is its use. The owner got it as a gift when they started at a new school. So the bag holds a memory too. Older people taught the makers the pattern. For them, it shows a skill. Each person has a different perspective. The context helps us see more. Context means who made it, who uses it, and why.

sections.heading: Objects carry meaning around the world
sections.text: Many communities make objects with cultural meaning. In Ghana, weavers make kente cloth from narrow strips that are sewn together. Many kente patterns have names, and some names come from proverbs or events in history. In Indonesia, people decorate batik cloth with hot wax and dye. Batik is used through life, from cloths that carry babies to clothes for weddings. In the Pacific, in places such as Tonga and Fiji, people beat tree bark to make tapa cloth. Groups often make it together, and it is used at weddings and other big events.
sections.simpler: Many groups make things with cultural meaning. In Ghana, people weave kente cloth. Many kente patterns have names. Some names come from wise words or past events. In Indonesia, people make batik with wax and dye. They use it for babies and at weddings. In the Pacific, people make tapa cloth from tree bark. Groups often make it together. They use it at big events.

sections.heading: Ask before you explain an object
sections.text: A museum label tells visitors about an object. The first label for the bag says only “Everyday carrying bag”. That is true, but it misses the memory and the skill. It is also a mistake to guess what the pattern means. A label that calls the pattern a symbol of a whole community, with no source, is weak. People in one group may not all see an object in the same way. A better label uses evidence from the makers and users. It says what we know and what we still need to ask.
sections.simpler: A museum label tells people about a thing. This label says “Everyday carrying bag”. That is true. But it misses the memory and the skill. Do not guess what the pattern means. Do not call it a symbol of a whole group. You need proof for that. A good label uses what the makers and users say. It also says what we still need to ask.

glossary.definition: The way one person sees or thinks about something.
glossary.example: From the owner's perspective, the bag holds a memory of a new school.

glossary.definition: The facts around something, such as who, where and why.
glossary.example: The bag's context includes who made it and who uses it.

glossary.definition: A person who creates something with their hands or tools.
glossary.example: The makers of the bag learned the pattern from older weavers.

glossary.definition: Linked to the shared ways of life of a group.
glossary.example: Kente patterns have cultural meaning in Ghana.

glossary.definition: A picture or shape that stands for an idea.
glossary.example: We should not call the bag's pattern a symbol without asking the makers.

checks.question: Which fact about the bag comes straight from the evidence?

options.text: The pattern means the same thing to everyone.
options.feedback: Not quite. No note says what the pattern means. Look at the seller's note.

options.text: The seller says it carries food and books.
options.feedback: Yes. The seller's note says the bag is made for carrying food and books.

options.text: The owner does not really like the bag.
options.feedback: Not quite. The owner got the bag as a gift and still has it. Look at the seller's note.

checks.question: What makes a museum label stronger?

options.text: It guesses what the pattern means.
options.feedback: Not quite. A guess is not evidence. The lesson says to ask the makers and users.

options.text: It uses as few words as it can.
options.feedback: Not quite. “Everyday carrying bag” is short, but it misses the memory and the skill.

options.text: It uses what makers and users say.
options.feedback: Yes. A strong label uses evidence from the people who made and used the object.

checks.question: What question would you ask the craft group before you write the label?
checks.placeholder: For example: Where did you learn this pattern? What does it mean to you?

write.prompt: Write a better museum label for the woven bag. Say what it is used for, give one meaning from the evidence, and add one question for the makers.
sentenceStarters: Before we explain the pattern, we need to ask ...
selfCheck: I named what the bag is used for.
I gave one meaning from the evidence.
I wrote one question for the makers.
write.example: This bag is used for carrying food and books. For its owner, the bag is also a memory. An aunt gave it to them when they started at a new school. For the makers, the pattern shows a skill they learned from older weavers. Before we explain the pattern, we need to ask the craft group what it means to them. This shows that one object can have many meanings. A good label says whose view it is.

speak.partnerTask: One person says what the bag is used for. The other adds a different perspective, such as the owner's or the makers'.
speak.independentTask: Choose an object you know, or one from the lesson. Explain two different meanings it could have.

watch.title: How Are Everyday Things Made Special?
watch.channel: Ayala Museum, ATIN: Stories from the Collection
watch.why: This short museum video from the Philippines looks at everyday objects that carry skill, beauty and meaning.
watch.beforeQuestion: Can a useful object also tell a story?
watch.afterQuestion: Whose perspective would you ask for before you write a label for one of these objects?
watch.summary: This short video comes from the Ayala Museum in the Philippines. It looks at three everyday objects from the museum. The first is a small green pot from China. Long ago, people in the Philippines traded for Chinese pots and bowls. Most were plain, but this one has two dragons on it. The second is the salakot, a wide hat woven from plants. Many ordinary people wore it. But some salakot were decorated with shell and silver for important people. The third is a small cloth called a handkerchief. If you look closely, you can see a sad poem sewn into it. The video says the materials and the skill make an object valuable. But the stories and context around it make it even more special.
keyPoints: Everyday objects can carry skill, beauty and meaning.
Details, like dragons on a pot or a poem on a cloth, can make an object special.
The stories and context of an object make it even more valuable.

visual.description: The woven bag from the evidence in the centre, with a pattern of triangles and lines. Around it are three speech bubbles: the seller (“For carrying food and books”), the owner (“A gift when I started at a new school”) and the craft group (“Older weavers taught us this pattern”). Below the bag is a museum label that reads “Everyday carrying bag” with a large question mark next to it.

sensitiveNotes: Some learners may want to talk about objects from their own lives. Welcome this, but never ask for it: an object from the lesson always works as an answer.
educatorNotes: You could add a local example, such as a woven basket or printed cloth from your area, if someone who makes or uses it can explain it in their own words.
The main skill is telling apart what we know (from evidence) and what we would be guessing. Praise answers that say “we would need to ask”.
changes: Expanded the reading from about 90 to about 290 words, with real examples from Ghana (kente), Indonesia (batik) and the Pacific (tapa).
Rewrote simpler English at a much lower level, with one idea per sentence.
Added a warm-up, a craft group's note to the evidence (so the makers' view is present), a self-check list and a visual plan.
Fixed glossary words that never appeared in the text; all five now appear in both versions of one section.
Moved the correct answers out of the first position and rewrote all feedback.
Replaced the Ayala Museum playlist link in sources with specific pages; the lesson's video is still in Watch.
